text: Dress and Behavior Expected in Clinical AreaIn order to gain and maintain the trust and confidence of patients, there are certain rules of behavior that a doctor or medical student must observe. If your standards of dress and behavior are professional and reasonably conservative you will be unlikely to cause offence or anxiety to your patients, and you will find that your relationships with them and with hospital staff will be easier. Students should be dressed in an appropriate and professional manner whilst on hospitals wards, at clinical skills sessions with patients or simulated patients and at OSCEs. • White coats are mandatory or surgical scrub• No low cut tops, no bare midriffs • No stilettos • No wrist watches, bracelets or wrist bands • No jewellery Except: o Rings – one single metal band, no stones o Earrings – small studs only o Necklaces – a simple chain if tucked inside clothing • No piercings (other than earrings) • Hair kept neat and tidy, long hair tied back, modest hair coloring/highlights only • Fingernails short and clean, no false nails • No food and drinks will be allowed in skills lab.• No Photos and videos will be allowed in skills lab.

name: Vital Signs: Pulse
text: Review Learning Guides for Measuring Radial Pulse before clinical skills session on Vital Signs Radial Pulse Vital signs are indicators of the basic functions of the body. Any physiological or pathological changes in the body functions would be reflected in the vital signs . The four main vital signs routinely checked by healthcare providers include: Body temperature Pulse rate Breathing rate (respiration) Blood pressure We will start by pulse rate What is the pulse rate? Pulse Rate: is measuring heartbeat by palpating a peripheral artery with the fingertip. The pulse rate is a measurement of the heart rate. This is the number of times the heart beats per minute. As the heart pushes blood through the arteries, the arteries expand and contract with the blood flow . Taking a pulse not only measures the heart rate but also can indicate the following: Heart rhythm Strength of the pulse The normal pulse rate for healthy adults ranges from 60- 100 beats per minute. Exercises, some illnesses and emotions could increase the heart rate. On the other hand, runners who do a lot of cardiovascular conditions may have a slower heart rate of 40 beats per minute. Pulse could be recorded from accessible arteries such as: Carotid Temporal Brachial Radial How to measure Radial pulse ? STEP CP PA NP Getting ready Prepare equipment: Watch or clock with a counter for seconds. Wash hands Greet the patient, Stand on the right side, Introduce yourself to the patient, and Explain the procedure to the patient. Assist the patient to pronate and slightly fix the forearm on his chest. The procedure Use the right hand to palpate the patient's left radial pulse and vice versa. Locate the radial artery just medial to the distal radius and proximal to the patient’s wrist on the thumb side, about two centimeters proximal to the thenar eminence. Place the tips of the index, middle and ring fingers just proximal to the patient’s wrist on the thumb side, orienting them over the vessel. Push lightly at first, gradually adding pressure till you feel the pulse. Check for regularity: if regular, count the pulse rate for 15 seconds and multiply by 4, and if irregular, count for 3 minutes and divide by 3. After the procedure Wash the hands. Discuss the findings with the patient. Record the results as beats / minute and comment on regularity. Thank the patient. CP: Competently performed PA performed with Assistance NP ( not done)

Arterial Blood Pressure What is Blood Pressure Blood pressure is defined as the lateral pressure exerted by flowing blood on the walls of the arteries How is blood pressure measured? Blood pressure is measured in millimeters of mercury (mmHg) and is given as 2 figures: systolic pressure – the pressure when the heart pushes blood out diastolic pressure – the pressure when the heart rests between beats What are equipment needed for measuring blood pressure Sphygmomanometer There are different types of Sphygmomanometers Mercury Sphygmomanometer Mercury sphygmomanometers are made up of manually inflatable cuffs that are attached to measuring units with mercury-infused tubes. While operating the device, it is important to place the apparatus on a flat surface and in an upright position to get the correct readings. Aneroid Sphygmomanometer Aneroid means “without fluid,” and as the name suggests, this type of BP apparatus doesn’t make use of any mercury and is therefore considered the safest alternative to mercury sphygmomanometers. In the aneroid device, the cuff is attached to a dial gauge with tubing. The gauge head contains mechanical parts that convert the cuff pressure into gauge-based reading. Automatic Digital Sphygmomanometer The automatic digital sphygmomanometer is the most technologically-advanced sphygmomanometer design to date. These devices use an electronic pressure sensor to measure the blood pressure, and the readings are presented on a digital display. Similar to mercury and aneroid sphygmomanometers, digital sphygmomanometers also come with inflatable cuffs, but there is a difference in the procedure for measuring blood pressure. Unlike the other two types, automatic digital sphygmomanometers evaluate and measure the fluctuations of arteries. Stethoscope III. Measuring Blood Pressure STEP/TASK CP AP NP Getting ready: Wash your hand Introduce yourself to the patient. Explain the procedure and obtain his consent. Tell him that he might feel some discomfort as the cuff is inflated, and that the blood pressure measurement may have to be repeated. Position The patient should be in the sitting position after 5 minutes rest. Three parts should be supported: back, feet and the arm. Ask the patient to expose the right arm by rolling up sleeve Attaching Blood Pressure Cuff Check that the blood pressure cuff size is appropriate for the patient's arm and that it is fully deflated Confirm the location of the brachial artery by palpating medial to the biceps brachii tendon and lateral to the medial epicondyle of the humerus Wrap the blood pressure cuff around the patient's upper arm, 2 cm above the antecubital fossa. Measuring blood pressure Position the BP measuring device so that it is roughly at the level of the patient’s heart. Position the measurement column/dial so that it is at eye level. Position the patient's right arm so that it is horizontal at the level of the midsternal and free from obstructive clothing. Measuring Blood Pressure Palpatory method Palpate the patient’s radial pulse, Inflate the blood pressure cuff until you can no longer feel the patient's radial pulse. Note the reading on the sphygmomanometer at the point at which the radial pulse becomes impalpable. This reading is an approximate estimate of the patient's systolic blood pressure Open the valve and deflate the blood pressure cuff Close the valve on the blood pressure cuf f Measuring Blood Pressure Auscultatory Method Place the stethoscope over the brachial artery pulse, ensuring that it does not touch the cuff. Inflate the cuff to 20-30 mmHg more than the estimated systolic blood pressure (obliteration pressure). Then slowly deflate the cuff at around 2-3 mmHg per second The first consistent Korotkov sounds indicate the systolic blood pressure. The muffling and disappearance of the Korotkov sounds indicate the diastolic blood pressure. Record the blood pressure as the systolic reading over the diastolic reading. If the blood pressure is higher than 140/90, indicate that you might take a second reading after giving the patient a one minute rest. If the patient has a history of postural hypotension. you must also record the standing blood pressure To complete the procedure Once the blood pressure has been obtained, remove the blood pressure cuf f. text: The electroencephalogram (EEG) is a measurement that enables us to detect the generalized activity of the cerebral cortex. Recorded from the surface of the scalp. The human EEG was first described by Austrian Psychiatrist Hans Berger in 1929. Electro Electrical encephalo Brain gram Picture Beta waves are observed in all age groups. They tend to be small in amplitude and usually are symmetric and more evident anteriorly. Beta is a ‘fast’ activity, present when we are alert, attentive , engaged in problem solving, judgment, decision making, and engaged in focused mental activity. Beta waves (12 to 30 Hz) Theta waves (3 to 8 Hz) Theta waves normally are seen in sleep at any age. In awake adults, these waves are abnormal if they occur in excess. Theta and delta waves are known collectively as slow waves. Theta brainwaves occur most often in sleep but are also dominant in deep meditation. Delta waves (3 Hz or less) They normally are seen in deep sleep , in adults as well as in infants and children. They have the largest amplitude of all waves. Delta brainwaves are slow, loud brainwaves. Brain produced all these waves all times, only the strength of the signal is dependent on the type of activity we are engaged in. K complex K complex waves are large-amplitude delta frequency waves, sometimes with a sharp apex. It signalling the onset of Stage N2 sleep Sleep spindles Like K-complexes, sleep spindles mark the onset of Stage N2 sleep and are usually seen against a generally slowed background. THANK YOU Collective synchronous activity of thousands of neurons are needed to create an EEG wave. They are signals generated when neurons send message to another. The quicker the firing, higher frequency of wave The more the neuron firing, more amplitude of the wave. EEG Rhythms Recording Brain Waves Recording an EEG is relatively simple, noninvasive, and it is painless. 24 or so electrodes taped to scalp at standard positions. they are fixed to standard positions on the head. and connected to banks of amplifiers and recording devices. TROPHIC & VASOMOTOR CHANGES 10. SKULL & SPINE EXAINATION 11. SPECIAL TESTS 12. GENERAL EXAMINATION A. General appearance and behavior  Physical development will indicate any gross endocrinal or nutritional disturbance. e.g. height, weight ▪ General appearance may be very helpful for early diagnosis, as the expressionless face of parkinsonism syndrome which may be evident before the appearance of the disease ▪ Age and concordance of appearance to age, Body build, Posture, Eye contact, Dress/grooming ▪ Alertness/attentiveness to the examiner: Physical features/abnormalities, Emotional facial expression ▪ General motor status: Retardation, Agitation, Abnormal movements, Gait  Pallor, jaundice etc. Neurologic examination 4 B. Mental state examination 1) State of consciousness Glasgow coma scale is the standard and should be assessed in every patient Glasgow Coma Scale 2) Intellectual functions I. Orientation (awareness to)  Person  Place  Time II. Attention & concentration  Ask the patient to Ability to count by serial 7‘s (subtract serial 7s from 100).  Ask the patient to name five things that start with a particular letter.  Ask the patient to rename days of week backward.  Ability to spell a word backward and forward III. Memory  Remote memory: ask about childhood data, important events known to have occurred when the patient was younger or free of illness.  Recent memory: the past few days what the patient had for breakfast, lunch, dinner.  Immediate retention or recall: digit span measures; ability to repeat six figures after examiner; ability to repeat three words 3 simple objects after 2 and 5 minutes (dog – cat – street) IV. Intelligence: mathematical problem- Educational and professional achievements (Average versus above average/below average) V. Insight: Awareness of the illness and its implications VI. Judgment: Ability to satisfactorily resolve a proposed hypothetical scenario utilizing good judgment VII. General knowledge Neurologic examination 5 3) Mood, Affect & Emotion Stability, Range, Appropriateness, Intensity, Mood (Experience and Expression) Behavior (expression): Aggressive, assertive, passive, and passive aggressive. Thought content: Suicidal ideation, Homicidal ideation, Depressive cognitions, Obsessions, Ruminations, Phobias, Ideas of reference, Paranoid ideation, Delusions C. Speech & articulation  Disturbance of speech is called, according to its severity, dysphasia or aphasia  Disturbance of articulation is called dysarthria, or anarthria  Speech examination: 1. Spontaneous speech a. Informal interview: Attention should be paid to the fluency of speech, presence of initiation difficulty, the presence of word-finding pauses. b. Structured task 2. Naming objects: tested by asking the patient to name objects, object parts, pictures, colors, or body parts to confrontation. 3. Repetition: Repetition of words and phrases should be deliberately tested. 4. Reading 5. Writing Simplified examination:  Receptive:  Auditory: Give the patient orders to do: start with one order then 2 orders, then 3 integrated complex orders  Visual: Give the patients the same orders written on the paper and tell him to do it.  Expressive Naming objects  Spoken.  Written. Types of aphasia or dysphasia:  Expressive aphasia (=motor=Broca‘s aphasia)  Receptive aphasia (=sensory =Wernicke‘s aphasia)  Global aphasia: no reception & no expression  Nominal aphasia: cannot name objects  Alexia: cannot read  Agraphia: cannot write.  Articulation examination: الفااححت alfatiha) Read  Repeating a long word with multiple syllables: أسكٌدريت  Count from 1-100 Neurologic examination 6 Dysarthria means only faulty articulation of speech sounds. It may result from central lesions of the brain or cerebellum, intoxications (such as alcohol), or neuromuscular disorders. Examiner should pay attention to different form of dysarthria for example slurred speech which occurs with lesions along the course of the pyramidal tr act, staccato or scanning speech which occurs in cerebellar lesion, low monotonous tone or nasal tone of voice etc. D. Cranial nerves examination The 12 pairs of cranial nerves (with the exception of the olfactory (I) pair and optic (II) pair arise from the brainstem). Cranial nerves II, III, IV and VI relate to the eye and the VIII nerve to hearing and balance. I. Olfactory nerve Function: Conveys the sense of smell. Examination: Ask the patient to close his eye. Test each nostril separately. Hold a non-irritant odor in front of the open nostril and ask him to sniff. Wait a moment for the patient to perceive the odor and then identify it. NB: Avoid the use of irritating substance as ammonia which will stimulate the trigeminal nerve. Abnormalities: Hyposmia (decreased sense of smell) or anosmia (inability to smell). Parosmia (the perception of pleasant odors as unpleasant).  The most frequent causes of anosmia are the common cold, COVID, allergic rhinitis, smoking, and head trauma.  Hyposmia also occurs in, Wernicke -Korsakoff syndrome, Kallman syndrome, Alzheimer‘s disease, Parkinson‘s disease and lesions of the olfactory bulbs and tracts like meningeal neoplasms- classically, olfactory groove meningiomas - that compress the olfactory bulbs and tracts. II. Optic nerve Function: vision The visual pathway consists of the retina, optic nerve, optic chiasm, optic tracts, lateral geniculate bodies, optic radiations and visual cortex. The pupil controls the amount of light entering the eye. For pupillary constriction, the afferent pathway is the optic nerve. Examination: • VISUAL ACUITY: Counting Finger-Snellen Chart • VISUAL FIELDS: by the confrontation method Take a distance of 1 meter between the doctor &patients Then check the field from the periphery, from the 4 directions • FUNDOSCOPIC EXAM: Optic disc - Optic cup – Retinal vessels Neurologic examination 7 Abnormalities: Deficits in the visual pathway lead to specific field defects (Total loss of vision in one eye because of a lesion of the optic nerve). III Oculomotor, IV Trochlear, VI Abducent nerves Function: The upper lid is elevated by the levator palpebrae superioris, innervated by cranial nerve III. The six extraocular muscles are responsible for eye movements. Cranial nerve III innervates the superior rectus, medial rectus, inferior oblique and inferior rectus muscles. Cranial nerve IV innervates the superior oblique muscle and cranial nerve VI innervates the lateral rectus muscle. Neurologic examination 8 Examination: 1. Palpebral fissures: detect any dropping of the upper eye lid (ptosis), or retraction of it. Also, observe the position of the eyes for any exophthalmos (proptosis) or enophthalmos. Detect any nystagmus in the position of rest. text: Brain Rhythm Abeer El- Emam Prof. of Physiology Alexandria Faculty of Medicine Alpha waves generally are seen in all age groups but are most common in adults. They tend to be present posteriorly more than anteriorly and are especially prominent with closed eyes and with relaxation. Alpha activity disappears normally with attention ( eg , mental arithmetic, stress, opening eyes). Alpha is the resting state for the brain. Alpha waves (8 to 12 Hz) Alpha wave (occipital) Beta waves are observed in all age groups. They tend to be small in amplitude and usually are symmetric and more evident anteriorly. Beta is a ‘fast’ activity, present when we are alert, attentive , engaged in problem solving, judgment, decision making, and engaged in focused mental activity. Beta waves (12 to 30 Hz) Theta waves (3 to 8 Hz) Theta waves normally are seen in sleep at any age. In awake adults, these waves are abnormal if they occur in excess. Theta and delta waves are known collectively as slow waves. Theta brainwaves occur most often in sleep but are also dominant in deep meditation. Delta waves (3 Hz or less) They normally are seen in deep sleep , in adults as well as in infants and children. They have the largest amplitude of all waves. Delta brainwaves are slow, loud brainwaves. Brain produced all these waves all times, only the strength of the signal is dependent on the type of activity we are engaged in. Slow Wave (or non-REM) Sleep Stage 1,2,3 REM-Sleep. STAGES OF SLEEP 17-Nov-25 15 17-Nov-25 16 K complex K complex waves are large-amplitude delta frequency waves, sometimes with a sharp apex. It signalling the onset of Stage N2 sleep Sleep spindles Like K-complexes, sleep spindles mark the onset of Stage N2 sleep and are usually seen against a generally slowed background. K complex Sleep spindle EXPERIMENTAL OBJECTIVES To record EEG from an awake, resting subject with their eyes open and eyes closed To observe interruptions of alpha rhythm during performance of mental math To observe temporary interruptions of alpha rhythm, following opening of the eye To identify and examine the alpha, beta, delta, and theta components of the EEG complex. Recording Brain Waves Recording an EEG is relatively simple, noninvasive, and it is painless. 24 or so electrodes taped to scalp at standard positions. they are fixed to standard positions on the head. and connected to banks of amplifiers and recording devices. Recording Brain Waves Measurements of individual neurons is not possible from the scalp, but the activity of collections of neurons is possible. Categorization of rhythms based on frequency. Sites of Electrode Placement MATERIALS BIOPAC electrode lead set (SS2L) BIOPAC Disposable Electrodes (EL503,) 3 electrodes per subject BIOPAC Electrode Gel (GEL1) and Abrasive Pad (ELPAD) or Skin cleanser or alcohol prep Biopac Student Lab System: BSL 4 software, MP36, MP35 or MP45 hardware Computer system (Windows or Mac) Hints for obtaining optimal data  As much as possible, move the hair away from the electrode area to ensure the electrode makes contact with the scalp.  Apply some gel to the electrode.  Apply pressure to the electrodes for about 1 minute after the initial placement.  Subject must remain still. Blinking and other movement will affect the recording of all four rhythms. Recording 1- Relaxed with eyes closed Recording 2- Performing mental math with eyes closed Recording 3- Relaxed with eyes open Recording 4- Subject hyperventilates (by breathing rapidly and deeply through mouth) for two minutes with eyes closed. Recording steps Instruct the Subject to relax with eyes closed, not thinking about anything (not fixing attention on any mental object). Click "Start" to begin recording. Continue recording and observe the corresponding plot, primarily expressing alpha rhythm, for one or two minutes. Press the F9 key to insert a marker while telling the Subject to open his eyes. Wait a few seconds and then insert another marker while telling the Subject to close his eyes. Tell the Subject to close his eyes and relax. Inform the Subject that he will be asked to perform mental math. Example: Count backward from 30 by subtracting increasing odd numbers (e.g., 30, 29, 26, 21). Running the Experiments Subject hyperventilates (by breathing rapidly and deeply through mouth) for two minutes with eyes closed. recording is resumed as quickly as possible after Subject has hyperventilated. However, to avoid EMG artifact, make sure Subject has stopped hyperventilating prior to clicking Record. As soon as Subject stops hyperventilating and is sitting still, Click Record immediately. Record for 10 seconds. Click Suspend. Hyperventilation evoke generalized slowing of EEG and elicit any abnormality When a person hyperventilates (breathes rapidly and deeply), too much carbon dioxide is eliminated from the blood, causing the blood and the cerebrospinal fluid that bathes the brain to become too alkaline. These changes increase the overall electrical activity of the brain including the amplitude of alpha waves Recording after hyperventilation The brain is continually active, even in the absence of environmental and body derived stimuli. Brain Rhythm Recording after hyperventilation Recording during mental math Alpha block THANK YOU The electroencephalogram (EEG) is a measurement that enables us to detect the generalized activity of the cerebral cortex. Recorded from the surface of the scalp. The human EEG was first described by Austrian Psychiatrist Hans Berger in 1929. Electro Electrical encephalo Brain gram Picture Collective synchronous activity of thousands of neurons are needed to create an EEG wave. They are signals generated when neurons send message to another. The quicker the firing, higher frequency of wave The more the neuron firing, more amplitude of the wave. EEG Rhythms The extracellular voltage change within the cortex which recorded by scalp electrodes is largely derived from the excitatory and inhibitory post-synaptic potentials (EPSPs and IPSPs ), not from the neuronal action potentials. This is because, although action potentials are of much greater voltage, they are very brief , whereas the EPSPs and IPSPs are of much longer duration and hence, can summate to create a signal capable of being detected on the surface of the scalp through the resistance of the overlying tissues. Power is defined as the amount of work done per unit time. Dynamometry means the measurement of power (dyno= power, meter = measure,) of muscle clenches by a hand dynamometer equipped with an electronic transducer. Meanwhile, fatigue can be induced by performing repetitive acute maximum work. Electromyography is a technique for evaluating and recording the electrical activity produced by skeletal muscles. It assess both muscle and nerve function. EMG is performed using an instrument called an electromyograph to produce a record called an electromyogram. Integrated EMG is an alternative view of the EMG signal that shows a more accurate pattern of muscle activity. 4- To test the muscle power (measured in Kg) from the dominant arm, perform a series of Clench-Release-Wait cycles until maximum grip force is reached by holding clench for two seconds, release for two seconds and completely relax grip force between clenches. Spontaneous activity There is no spontaneous activity in normal muscle , with the exclusion of potentials that could be recorded if the needle is positioned near a neuromuscular junction (end-plate noise and end-plate spikes ). In myopathic disorders, abnormal spontaneous potentials such as fibrillations and positive sharp waves are seen. Fibrillations and positive sharp waves are potentials that are generated by individual muscle fibers. 2. To generate force with minimal contraction, many motor units are getting activated earlier than expected. This is described as an early or rapid recruitment pattern and is typical for myopathic processes. Premature activation of motor units during minimal effort, or inappropriate firing of many MUAPs to generate a small amount of force typically indicating myopathy.
